sources.text:
Software Attack - Malwares
•
Cybercriminals may use different types of 
malicious software, or malware, to carry out 
their activities. 
•
A malware also can be defined as “a program 
that is inserted into a system, usually covertly, 
with the intent of compromising the 
confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the 
victim’s data, applications, or operating 
system or otherwise annoying or disrupting 
the victim.”  - NIST 800-83
Photo by Sander Weeteling on Unsplash

Types of Malwares (cont.)
Virus
a type of computer program 
that, when executed, 
replicates and attaches itself 
to other executable files. 
spread by USB drives, optical 
disks, network shares or 
email.
Worms
malware that replicates itself 
in order to spread from one 
computer to another. 
Unlike a virus, which requires 
a host program to run, 
worms can run by 
themselves. (Self Propagate)
Trojan Horse
malware that carries out 
malicious operations by 
masking its true intent.
Might appear legitimate but 
is, in fact, very dangerous. 
e.g. image files, audio files, 
games, or mobile apps.

Types of Malwares (cont.)
Spyware
Designed to track and spy 
infected system, monitors online 
activity and can log every key 
press on your keyboard.
Often bundles itself with 
legitimate software or Trojan 
horses.
Adware
Often installed with some 
versions (3rd parties) of software 
and is designed to automatically 
deliver advertisements to a user. 
It is common for adware to come 
with spyware.
Scareware
A type of malware that uses 
'scare’ tactics to trick you into 
taking a specific action.  
(Social Engineering)
If you agree to execute the 
specific program, your system will 
become infected with malware.

Types of Malwares (cont.)
Backdoor
Type of malware is used to gain 
unauthorized access by bypassing 
the normal authentication 
procedures.
Hackers can gain remote access 
to resources within an application 
and issue remote system 
commands.
Rootkit
Designed to modify the operating 
system to create a backdoor, 
which attackers can then use to 
access your computer remotely.
Can modify system forensics and 
monitoring tools, making them 
very hard to detect.
Ransomware
Designed to hold a computer 
system or the data it contains 
captive until a payment is made.
Often spread through phishing 
emails that encourage you to 
download a malicious attachment 
or through a software 
vulnerability.

machines by intercepting

enforcing policy;
•
Security awareness training: instructs employees on security best practices -- this includes education on 
potential security threats, such as phishing, and computer security best practices for using company devices; and

improvements will be made.

Threat Modelling
•
Threat modeling is the practice of systematically

contexts above and beyond the technical attack 
surfaces.

manipulate model inputs, poison training data, or 
exploit biases.
•
Accomplish threat modeling by carefully examining a 
model’s architecture, data flows, and interactions to 
pinpoint where the threats might emerge and 
determine effective mitigation strategies. 
•
By building a comprehensive threat model, teams 
can prioritize mitigation efforts—whether it’s filtering 
harmful content, strengthening data validation, or 
securing model deployment pipelines
According to the Threat Modeling Manifesto, this process 
involves answering four questions:
1. What are we working on? (Model the system architecture)
2. What can go wrong? (Identify/Enumerate threats)
3. What are we going to do about it? (Determine mitigations)
4. Did we do a good enough job? (Validate and iterate)

Cyberwarfare
The profile of a cyber attacker varies depending on their 
goals, motivations and capabilities. 
At the extreme, hackers can launch cyber-attacks against 
nations and states, wreaking havoc on their computer 
systems and networks.
The main reason for resorting to cyberwarfare is to gain 
advantage over adversaries, whether they are nations or 
competitors.
•
To gather compromised information and/or defense 
(military) secrets.
•
To impact another nation’s infrastructure.
Photo by Patrick Federi on Unsplash

Vulnerabilities
•
Leaky (loss of confidentiality)
–
e.g. data breach, data stolen, identity theft … 
•
Corrupted (loss of integrity)
–
e.g. unauthorized change of information 
•
Unavailable or very slow (loss of availability)
–
e.g. DDoS attack, file deletion etc…

Cyber Threats
•
“Any circumstance or event with the potential 
to adversely impact organizational 
operations, organizational assets, or 
individuals through an information system via 
unauthorized access, destruction, disclosure, 
modification of information, and/or denial of 
service” – NIST-IR 7298
•
Capable of exploiting vulnerabilities
•
Represent potential security harm to an asset

Types of Threat
Internal
•
Employee, Contract Staff, 
Partners
•
Mishandle data, uses 
infected USB drive, clicked 
malicious email / website 
links
External
•
Amateur / skilled attackers 
outside the organization
•
Exploit vulnerable networks
•
Gain unauthorized access 
to application or devices
•
Social Engineering

Threat Consequences and Threat Actions
Threat Consequence
Threat Action (Attack)
Unauthorized Disclosure
A circumstance or event 
whereby an entity gains access 
to data for which the entity is 
not authorized.
Exposure: Sensitive data are directly released to an unauthorized entity.
Interception: An unauthorized entity directly accesses sensitive data traveling 
between authorized sources and destinations.
Inference: A threat action whereby an unauthorized entity indirectly accesses 
sensitive data (but not necessarily the data contained in the communication) 
by reasoning from characteristics or by-products of communications.
Intrusion: An unauthorized entity gains access to sensitive data by 
circumventing a system’s security protections.
Deception
A circumstance or event that 
may result in an authorized 
entity receiving false data and 
believing it to be true.
Masquerade: An unauthorized entity gains access to a system or performs a 
malicious act by posing as an authorized entity.
Falsification: False data deceive an authorized entity.
Repudiation: An entity deceives another by falsely denying responsibility for 
an act.
Stallings & Brown (2018), Table 1.2

Threat Consequences and Threat Actions
Threat Consequence
Threat Action (Attack)
Disruption
A circumstance or event that 
interrupts or prevents the 
correct operation of system 
services and functions.
Incapacitation: Prevents or interrupts system operation by disabling a system 
component.
Corruption: Undesirably alters system operation by adversely modifying 
system functions or data.
Obstruction: A threat action that interrupts delivery of system services by 
hindering system operation.
Usurpation
A circumstance or event that 
results in control of system 
services or functions by an 
unauthorized entity.
Misappropriation: An entity assumes unauthorized logical or physical control 
of a system resource.
Misuse: Causes a system component to perform a function or service that is 
detrimental to system security.
Stallings & Brown (2018), Table 1.2

Attack Surface Categories

Malwares
•
Malware is any code that can be used

or cause harm to or compromise a 
system in terms of its confidentiality, 
integrity and availability.

containing and removing them.

A worldwide cyberattack (ransomware) in

extort money.
•
Encrypting valuable files, so owner could 
not access them, or by locking out of their 
computer.
•
Takes data/system hostage, promising to

vulnerability in the SMB file sharing

•
A general term for attack types which consist 
of injecting code/script/command that is then 
interpreted/executed by the application.
•
Exploits poor handling of untrusted data and a 
lack of proper input/output data validation.
•
Usually made possible due poor input 
handling and commonly exploited over the

•

2025

Social engineers often rely on people’s willingness to be 
helpful, but they also prey on their weaknesses.
•
In short, “Tricking” users to assist in the compromise of their 
own systems

sources.text:
SECURITY POLICY
What is the security scheme supposed to do?

Why do we need Security Policy?
•
Security policies are important because they protect an 
organizations' assets, both physical and digital. 
•
Helps to identify all company assets and all threats to those 
assets.
•
Describe how these assets can be protected and how 
threats can be mitigated.
•
Guard reputations & ensure compliance with legal and 
regulatory requirements.
–
For example, Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI-DSS) 
dictates how organizations handle consumer payment card information. 
–
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) details how 
companies handle protected health information. Violating these regulations 
can be costly.

NTU – Acceptable IT Usage Policy
•
https://www.ntu.edu.sg/life-at-
ntu/internet-account-and-
policy/acceptable-it-usage-
policy

SECURITY IMPLEMENTATION
Preventive Measure & Requirements

Security & Risk Management
Planning: 
•
Develop, document, periodically update, and implement security plans for organizational information systems that describe 
the security controls in place or planned for the information systems and the rules of behavior for individuals accessing the 
information systems.
Systems and Services Acquisition:
•
Allocate sufficient resources to adequately protect organizational information systems;
•
employ system development life cycle processes that incorporate information security considerations (i.e. DevSecOps);
•
employ software usage and installation restrictions; and
•
ensure that third-party providers employ adequate security measures to protect information, applications, and/or services 
outsourced from the organization.
System and Communications Protection:
•
Monitor, control, and protect organizational communications (i.e., information transmitted or received by organizational 
information systems) at the external boundaries and key internal boundaries of the information systems; and
•
employ architectural designs, software development techniques, and systems engineering principles that promote effective 
information security within organizational information systems.

Security & Risk Management (Cont.)
Risk Assessment: 
•
Periodically assess the risk to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, or reputation), 
organizational assets, and individuals, resulting from the operation of organizational information systems and the 
associated processing, storage, or transmission of organizational information.
Contingency Planning: 
•
Establish, maintain, and implement plans for emergency response, backup operations, and post disaster recovery 
for organizational information systems to ensure the availability of critical information resources and continuity of 
operations in emergency situations.

Secure System Development
Identification and Authentication: 
•
Identify information system users, processes acting on behalf of users, or devices, and authenticate (or 
verify) the identities of those users, processes, or devices, as a prerequisite to allowing access to 
organizational information systems.
Access Control: 
•
Limit information system access to authorized users, processes acting on behalf of authorized users, or 
devices (including other information systems) and to the types of transactions and functions that 
authorized users are permitted to exercise.
Audit and Accountability:
•
Create, protect, and retain information system audit records to the extent needed to enable the 
monitoring, analysis, investigation, and reporting of unlawful, unauthorized, or inappropriate information 
system activity; and
•
ensure that the actions of individual information system users can be uniquely traced to those users so 
they can be held accountable for their actions.

Secure Operation
Physical and Environmental Protection:
•
Limit physical access to information systems, equipment, and the respective operating environments to authorized 
individuals;
•
protect the physical plant and support infrastructure for information systems;
•
provide supporting utilities for information systems;
•
protect information systems against environmental hazards; and
•
provide appropriate environmental controls in facilities containing information systems.
Configuration Management:
•
Establish and maintain baseline configurations and inventories of organizational information systems (including hardware, 
software, firmware, and documentation) throughout the respective system development life cycles; and
•
establish and enforce security configuration settings for information technology products employed in organizational 
information systems.
Maintenance:
•
Perform periodic and timely maintenance on organizational information systems; and
•
provide effective controls on the tools, techniques, mechanisms, and personnel used to conduct information system 
maintenance.

Secure Operation (Cont.)
System and Information Integrity:
•
Identify, report, and correct information and information system flaws in a timely manner;
•
provide protection from malicious code at appropriate locations within organizational 
information systems; and
•
monitor information system security alerts and advisories and take appropriate actions in 
response.
Incident Response:
•
Establish an operational incident-handling capability for organizational information systems 
that includes adequate preparation, detection, analysis, containment, recovery, and user-
response activities; and
•
track, document, and report incidents to appropriate organizational officials and/or 
authorities.

Security Compliance & Governance
Certification, Accreditation, and Security Assessments:
•
Periodically assess the security controls in organizational information 
systems to determine if the controls are effective in their application;
•
develop and implement plans of action designed to correct deficiencies and 
reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in organizational information systems;
•
authorize the operation of organizational information systems and any 
associated information system connections; and
•
monitor information system security controls on an ongoing basis to ensure 
the continued effectiveness of the controls.

Secure Computer User
Awareness and Training:
•
Ensure that managers and users of organizational information systems are made aware of the security risks associated with 
their activities and of the applicable laws, regulations, and policies related to the security of organizational information 
systems; and
•
ensure that personnel are adequately trained to carry out their assigned information security-related duties and 
responsibilities.
Personnel Security:
•
Ensure that individuals occupying positions of responsibility within organizations (including third-party service providers) are 
trustworthy and meet established security criteria for those positions;
•
ensure that organizational information and information systems are protected during and after personnel actions such as 
terminations and transfers; and
•
employ formal sanctions for personnel failing to comply with organizational security policies and procedures.
Media Protection:
•
Protect information system media, both paper and digital;
•
limit access to information on information system media to authorized users; and
•
sanitize or destroy information system media before disposal or release for reuse.

PREVENTION & MITIGATION
Organization, Systems, People

Defense Mechanism (Techniques)
Context
Techniques / Tools
Applicable for
Software / System Security
Authentication, Authorization, & Encryption
Access control for data and systems 
(confidentiality & integrity)
Deployment & Integration
Penetration Testing
Vulnerability assessment
Network
Firewall, Intrusion Detection & Prevention 
Systems (IDS/IPS)
Network defense & monitoring
Cloud & IoT
Professional Trainings, Risk Assessments
Service availability & data
Human
Training & Awareness
End User, Employee, Business Partner
Operation
Security Information & Event Management 
(SIEM), Security, Orchestrion, Automation, 
& Response (SOAR)
Monitoring, threat hunting, & incident 
respond, forensics investigation

Software Security by Developers
Source: https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/2023/08/deloitte-safeguards-software-development-lifecycle/

Authentication
•
Derived Security Requirements:
1.
Use multifactor authentication for local and network access to privileged accounts and for 
network access to non-privileged accounts.
2.
Employ replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to privileged and 
non-privileged accounts.
3.
Prevent reuse of identifiers for a defined period.
4.
Disable identifiers after a defined period of inactivity.
5.
Enforce a minimum password complexity and change of characters when new passwords 
are created.
6.
Prohibit password reuse for a specified number of generations.
7.
Allow temporary password use for system logons with an immediate change to a permanent 
password.
8.
Store and transmit only cryptographically-protected passwords.
9.
Obscure feedback of authentication information.

Authentication
The four means of authenticating user identity are based on:
Something the individual knows
• Password, PIN, answers to prearranged questions
Something the individual possesses/have (token)
• Smartcard, electronic keycard, physical key
Something the individual is (static biometrics)
• Fingerprint, retina, face
Something the individual does (dynamic biometrics)
• Voice pattern, handwriting, typing rhythm

Authentication
•
Single sign-on (SSO) is a technology 
which combines several different application 
login screens into one. 
•
A user only has to enter their login 
credentials (username, password, etc.) one 
time on a single page to access all of their 
SaaS applications.
•
SSO protocols: Security Assertion Markup 
Language (SAML), OAuth 2.0 (OAuth2), 
OpenID Connect and etc…
Image Source: MiniOrange

Authorization
•
Basic Security Requirements
1.
Limit information system access to authorized users, processes acting on behalf 
of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems).
2.
Limit information system access to the types of transactions and functions that 
authorized users are permitted to execute.

Authorization
•
Derived Security Requirements
1.
Control the flow of controlled unclassified information (CUI) in accordance with 
approved authorizations.
2.
Separate the duties of individuals to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without 
collusion.
3.
Employ the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and 
privileged accounts.
4.
Use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing nonsecurity functions.
5.
Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and audit the 
execution of such functions.
6.
Limit unsuccessful logon attempts.
7.
Provide privacy and security notices consistent with applicable CUI rules.

Authorization
•
Derived Security Requirements (Cont.)
8.
Use session lock with pattern-hiding displays to prevent access and viewing of 
data after period of inactivity.
9.
Terminate (automatically) a user session after a defined condition.
10. Monitor and control remote access sessions.
11. Employ cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote 
access sessions.
12. Route remote access via managed access control points.
13. Authorize remote execution of privileged commands and remote access to 
security-relevant information.
14. Authorize wireless access prior to allowing such connections.

Authorization
•
Derived Security Requirements (Cont.)
15. Protect wireless access using authentication and encryption.
16. Control connection of mobile devices.
17. Encrypt CUI on mobile devices.
18. Verify and control/limit connections to and use of external information systems.
19. Limit use of organizational portable storage devices on external information 
systems.
20. Control CUI posted or processed on publicly accessible information systems.

Authorization - Access Control Policies
• Controls access based on the identity of the requestor and on access rules 
(authorizations) stating what requestors are (or are not) allowed to do
Discretionary access control 
(DAC)
• Controls access based on comparing security labels with security 
clearances
Mandatory access control 
(MAC)
• Controls access based on the roles that users have within the system and 
on rules stating what accesses are allowed to users in given roles
Role-based access control 
(RBAC)
• Controls access based on attributes of the user, the resource to be 
accessed, and current environmental conditions
Attribute-based access 
control (ABAC)

Authentication & Authorization

sources.text:
Types of Encryptions
Symmetric (Private Key) Encryption 
•only one key, and all communicating parties use the same (secret) key for both encryption and decryption.
•Examples: Data Encryption Standard (DES), 3-DES, Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
Asymmetric (Public Key) encryption
•two keys: one key is used for encryption, and a different key is used for decryption. 
•The decryption key is kept private (hence the "private key" name), while the encryption key is shared 
publicly, for anyone to use (hence the "public key" name)
•Examples: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman (RSA), Digital Signature Standard (D S S), Elliptic curve cryptography 
(ECC) …

Types of Encryptions (Cont.)
Symmetric (Private Key) Encryption

Network Security - Firewall
•
Designed to control or filter which 
communications are allowed in and out of a 
device or network based on specified security 
policies.
•
Filtering criteria includes IP address ranges, 
protocols, applications (ports) and content types
•
can be installed on 
–
a single computer (host-based firewall) 
–
standalone network device (network-based firewall).
–
Multi-layer
Stallings & Brown (2018), 
Figure 9.2

Network Security - Demilitarized Zone (DMZ)
•
A kind of subnetwork containing an 
organization's exposed, outward-facing 
services.
•
The systems in the DMZ are require or 
foster external connectivity, such as a 
corporate website, an e-mail server, or a 
DNS (domain name system) server.
Stallings & Brown (2018),

Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
•
Scan and monitor network traffic against 
rules or attack signatures for malicious 
traffic.
•
If match, IPS will log the event and notify 
network administrator, no other action 
(countermeasure) will be performed.
•
In short, IPS is responsible to monitor, 
detect, log, and report event/incident 
(malicious traffics)
Image Source: CISCO

Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
•
Similar to IDS but can block or deny 
traffic if detected.
•
In short, IPS is responsible to monitor, 
detect, log, and report event/incident 
(malicious traffics)
Image Source: CISCO

Cloud Security (Risk & Countermeasures)
Abuse and nefarious use of cloud computing
•Stricter initial registration and validation processes
•Enhanced credit card fraud monitoring and coordination
•Comprehensive inspection of customer network traffic
•Monitoring public blacklists for one’s own network blocks
Insecure interfaces and APIs
•Analyzing the security model of CSP interfaces
•Ensuring that strong authentication and access controls are implemented in concert with encrypted transmission
•Understanding the dependency chain associated with the API
Malicious insiders
•Enforce strict supply chain management and conduct a comprehensive supplier assessment
•Specify human resource requirements as part of legal contract
•Require transparency into overall information security and management practices, as well as compliance reporting
•Determine security breach notification processes

Cloud Security (Risk & Countermeasures)
Shared technology issues
• Implement security best practices for installation/configuration
• Monitor environment for unauthorized changes/activity
• Promote strong authentication and access control for administrative access and operations
• Enforce SLAs for patching and vulnerability remediation
• Conduct vulnerability scanning and configuration audits
Data loss or leakage
• Implement strong A P I access control
• Encrypt and protect integrity of data in transit and at rest
• Analyze data protection at both design and run time
• Implement strong key generation, storage and management, and destruction practices

Cloud Security (Risk & Countermeasures)
Account or service hijacking
• Prohibit the sharing of account credentials between users and services
• Leverage strong two-factor authentication techniques where possible
• Employ proactive monitoring to detect unauthorized activity
• Understand CSP security policies and SLAs
Unknown risk profile
• Disclosure of applicable logs and data
• Partial/full disclosure of infrastructure details
• Monitoring and alerting on necessary information

IoT Security
•
MiniSec 
– an open-source security module that is part of the TinyOS operating 
system
– designed to be a link-level module that offers a high level of security, 
while simultaneously keeping energy consumption low and using 
very little memory

input, retrieved content, tool output, image, audio, or video 
content, intermediate reasoning, or persistent memory, alters 
the model's behavior in ways the application developer did not 
intend.
– Context Window Pooling – treat system prompt, user input, retrieved 
documents, tool outputs, conversation history, and memory as a single 
token stream,
– Memory Persistence - Long-term memory, a RAG corpus, a vector 
store, or a hosted memory service.
– Agentic Execution - drives tool calls (file system, shell, email, cloud 
APIs, MCP servers, sub-agents)

LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection Anatomy
•
A prompt-injection anatomy can be characterized along three 
axes.
– Delivery surface - how it reaches the model (direct input, 
retrieved content, tool output, tool connection channel, or 
persistent memory).
– Propagation behavior - how it spreads across time and 
boundaries (single-shot, multi-step kill-chain, cross-session 
through memory or RAG, or self-replicating across agents)
– Encoding - how the malicious instructions are represented in 
tokens or pixels (plain text, base64 or other obfuscation, invisible 
Unicode, multimodal or steganographic, low-resource language)

LLM01:2026 Types of Prompt Injection
•
Direct Prompt Injection: 
– intentional (a malicious user crafting a jailbreak) or 
– unintentional (a legitimate user pasting content that happens to contain 
conflicting instructions
•
Indirect Prompt Injection: The model ingests content from an 
external source that contains data which acts as prompt injection.
– Untrusted surfaces -  Public web pages, emails from unknown senders, 
search results.
– Semi-trusted surfaces. Issue titles in a public bug tracker, package 
READMEs and changelogs, third-party API responses
– Trusted surfaces. The developer's own repositories, databases, internal 
documents, and mail

LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection (Mitigation)
•
Prompt injection is intrinsic to current generative AI
•
no single reliable prevention mechanism exists today, a position consistent 
with NIST (2025), NCSC (2025)
•
Secure by Design: Design the surrounding system on the explicit 
assumption that the model's instruction boundary will eventually be 
bypassed, and constrain what the model is permitted to do, and what its 
outputs are permitted to reach, so a successful injection does not translate 
into a successful exploit.
•
Apply the controls below as defense-in-depth, since no single control is 
sufficient.
•
For agentic deployments, the least-privilege and capability-budgeting 
controls.
•
Different case handle differently, see OWASP Top Ten for LLM 2026

sources.text:
LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure
•
Occurs when an LLM-integrated system exposes confidential, 
regulated, privileged, or proprietary data through a channel the data 
subject, controller, or system owner did not authorize.
•
Example of disclosure surfaces: tool-call arguments, reasoning 
traces, retrieved chunks, multimodal output, logs, telemetry, 
embeddings, and observable inference properties

LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure
•A model, fine-tune, or LoRA adapter memorizes corpus content and later reproduces it verbatim or in recoverable form
Training-time. 
•The model discloses live context (system prompt, RAG chunks, files, tool outputs, memory, or another session's data),
Inference-time. 
•Fine-tuning, distillation, synthetic-data generation, gradients, SDKs, and observability move sensitive data into derived 
artifacts.
Pipeline-time. 
•Adversaries infer facts from externally measurable properties (token length under TLS, latency, log-probabilities, 
confidence, cache-hit signals) without receiving content.
Observation-time.

(Mitigation)

–

hygiene, Sanitize with classifier, not regex alone, budget queries per user, 
operational hygiene.

–

vector store protection, format preserving encryption, audit logging into SIEM 
etc…
•
Tier 3: Advance (regulated, classified, high-target)
–
Confidential Computing (with hardware), audit synthetic data against extractors, 
exercise a disclosure incident-response playbook etc…

M4-N018.title: LLM03: Excessive Agency
M4-N018.explanation: Excessive agency gives a model-driven system more autonomy, permissions or functionality than the task requires. Harm can follow when that authority is misused.

sources.text:
LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency
•
An LLM-based system is often granted a degree of agency by its 
developer 
•
the ability to call functions or interface with other systems via 
extensions (sometimes referred to as tools, skills or plugins by 
different vendors) to undertake actions in response to a 
prompt. 
•
Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging 
actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or 
manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the 
LLM to malfunction.

LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency (Mitigation)
•
Minimize Tools: Limit the extensions that LLM agents are allowed to call to only the minimum necessary. 
•
Minimize tool functionality: Limit the functions that are implemented in LLM extensions to the minimum 
necessary.
•
Avoid open-ended tools: Avoid the use of open-ended tools where possible (e.g., run a shell command, 
fetch a URL, etc.) and use tools with more granular functionality
•
Minimize tool permissions: Limit the permissions that LLM tools are granted to other systems to the 
minimum necessary in order to limit the scope of undesirable actions
•
Execute tools in user's context: Track user authorization and security scope to ensure actions taken 
on behalf of a user are executed on downstream systems in the context of that specific user, and with the 
minimum privileges necessary.
•
Require user approval: Use human-in-the-loop control to require a human to approve high-impact 
actions before they are taken.
•
Complete mediation: Implement authorization in logic rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an 
action is allowed or not.
•
Monitor tool use: Log and monitor the activity of LLM tools and downstream systems to identify where 
undesirable actions are taking place, and respond accordingly. 
•
Rate limiting: Establish thresholds around the invocation of tools and implement circuit breakers that 
halt, rate-limit or escalate for human review if those thresholds are exceeded.

LLM04:2026 Supply Chain

susceptible to vulnerabilities that affect the integrity of training data,

Bill of Materials (SBOM),
•
Only use models from verifiable sources and compensate for weak 
provenance with third-party integrity checks, signing, and file hashes.
•
Strictly monitor and audit collaborative model development environments.
•
Encrypt models deployed at the edge with integrity checks

M4-N026.title: Attack chains and phases
M4-N026.explanation: An attack chain connects multiple actions or phases. Mapping the chain helps explain how separate weaknesses can combine into a successful compromise.

sources.text:
MOTIVATION, SKILL, TACTICS, TECHNIQUE, 
TECHNOLOGY : ATTACK CHAINS
A more broader view

The Shift in the Cyber (AI) Battlefield
•
For decades, securing an enterprise meant defending its code, its networks, 
and its databases. But today, we build systems that learn from data, make 
autonomous decisions, and talk back to us. This shift has created an 
entirely new battlefield.
•
Adversaries no longer just look for bugs in your software; they exploit the 
math, the memory, and the trust inside your Artificial Intelligence. 
•
The MITRE ATLAS framework is the map of this new battlefield. 
–
To understand it, we cannot look at security incidents as isolated events. 
–
Instead, we must view them as a calculated, An example of 5-phase journey where 
the attacker moves stealthily from public web searches directly into the brain of our 
systems.

https://atlas.mitre.org/matrices/ATLAS 
UPDATED!!!

ATLAS MITRE
•
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems (ATLAS)
•
Navigate threats to AI systems through real-world insights
•
Covers 16 Tactics with more than 100 techniques.
•
Some tactics and techniques adapted from the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, 
Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK) matrix
–
a knowledge base that details the different tactics and techniques that adversaries, or cyber 
attackers, use as well as the platforms they target, based on observations of real attacks that 
have occurred.
•
Offer Mitigation & Case Studies as well
https://atlas.mitre.org/matrices/ATLAS

Attack Phases
Phases
Tactic Name
Key Focus / Examples
Preparation
Reconnaissance, Resource 
Development, Initial Access, AI 
Attack Adaptation
Targeting model accessibility, framework 
profiling, and initial footholds
Establishment
Execution, Persistence, Privilege 
Escalation, Defense Evasion
Gaining runtime code execution, manipulating 
long-term memories, and jailbreaking safety 
filters
Exploitation
Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral 
Movement, Collection
Harvesting API keys, searching file directories, 
and moving to broader networks
Objectives / 
Achievement
ML Attack Staging, Command & 
Control, Exfiltration, Impact
Testing offline proxy models, leaking private 
data, or disrupting critical system decisions

CHAIN ATTACK USING VARIOUS TACTICS
An Example of…

Phase 1: Outside In — Preparation & 
Groundwork
1
Reconnaissance
Role: The attacker maps out your AI 
footprint from the outside. They discover 
what foundation models you use, identify 
employee profiles on LinkedIn to spot your 
ML libraries (PyTorch, LangChain), and 
probe public API documentation.
Hand-off to Step 2: The insights collected 
(e.g., "they use an open-weights LLaMA 
model hosted on Hugging Face") dictate 
what tools the attacker must acquire.
2
Resource Development
Role: Using their reconnaissance intel, the 
adversary prepares their arsenal. They buy 
GPU compute, construct poisoned training 
datasets, build weaponized prompt 
injection payloads, or create fake 
GitHub/Hugging Face accounts to host 
backdoored model weights.
Hand-off to Step 3: The weaponized 
resources are now ready to be deployed 
against your organization's perimeter.
3
Initial Access
Role: Crossing the security perimeter. The 
attacker uses phishing, exploits an 
unpatched web vulnerability in your 
application frontend, or submits an 
untrusted PDF containing indirect prompt 
injection into an AI document-processing 
pipeline.
Hand-off to Step 4: The attacker now has a 
live connection inside your application 
layer, but they still need to interact with 
the underlying AI models.
4
AI/ML Model Access 
Role: Bridging standard IT access to the 
AI/ML layer. The attacker gains the ability 
to query the model (black-box access via 
authorized inference APIs) or acquires raw 
model weights/checkpoints (white-box 
access via exposed cloud buckets or 
internal repos).
Hand-off to Step 5: With access to the 
model, the attacker transitions from 
probing to executing active exploits on the 
infrastructure.
Before setting foot in your network, the adversary studies your architecture and builds 
custom attack infrastructure.

Phase 2: In-System Execution & Hardening the 
Foothold
5
Execution
Role: Running malicious code on the host 
machine. If an adversary uploads an untrusted 
model file serialized with unsafe libraries (like 
Python's pickle), loading those weights triggers 
arbitrary code execution on the GPU cluster. 
Alternatively, they trick an autonomous AI agent's 
code-interpreter or bash-tool into running shell 
scripts.
Hand-off: The moment unauthorized code runs,
host detection systems (EDR, safety guardrails) 
will try to flag it. The attacker must disguise their 
presence.
6
Defense Evasion
Role: Blinding the defenders and evading AI 
guardrails. The attacker uses text obfuscation 
(e.g., Base64, ASCII art, or multi-turn jailbreaks) to 
bypass content filters, or crafts Adversarial 
Examples (subtle noise in images) to fool 
computer vision models without raising alerts in 
monitoring dashboards.
Hand-off: Having bypassed defensive barriers, the 
attacker locks in their access so a server reboot or 
session reset doesn't lock them out.
7
Persistence
Role: Embedding themselves permanently. In 
conventional IT, this is a cron job or startup 
registry. In AI systems, it can take the form of 
Memory Poisoning—altering an AI agent's long-
term vector store or user profile memory so the 
agent continues to follow malicious instructions 
in future chat sessions.
Hand-off to Step 7: While persistence keeps the 
attacker in the door, low-level user or container 
privileges restrict what they can touch.
8
Privilege Escalation 
Role: Leveling up rights. The adversary exploits 
misconfigured container runtimes, elevates from 
an unprivileged web user to an admin, or tricks an 
LLM into accessing restricted service-account 
tokens and back-end tools that standard users are 
blocked from invoking.
Now that the adversary can touch the model and runtime, they aim to execute 
arbitrary code, bypass safety rails, and ensure they cannot be easily kicked out.

Phase 3: Internal Maneuvering — Discovery & 
Lateral Expansion
9
Discovery
Role: Mapping the internal terrain. The attacker 
inspects the AI agent’s available tools, inspects 
local file systems, queries connected vector 
databases, and checks what external cloud 
services the ML pipeline connects to.
Hand-off: The discovery phase highlights the 
locked doors that require authentication (e.g., 
database connection strings, S3 buckets, 
proprietary model endpoints).
10
Credential Access
Role: Stealing keys to those locked doors. The 
adversary queries RAG knowledge stores to 
search for leaked hardcoded passwords, extracts 
API keys stored in cleartext environment variables 
(OPENAI_API_KEY, HUGGINGFACE_HUB_TOKEN), 
or dumps cached memory.
Hand-off: Armed with legitimate internal 
credentials, the attacker no longer needs to 
exploit complex vulnerabilities to move around.
11
Lateral Movement 
Role: Pivoting across networks. Using stolen 
credentials or an overprivileged autonomous AI 
agent as a proxy, the attacker leaves the AI 
subnet and hops into critical enterprise 
networks—such as internal code repositories, 
production databases, or central cloud 
management consoles.
With durable, high-privilege access, the adversary explores your internal network to 
find where your most valuable data and models reside.

Phase 4: Staging & Command — Preparing the 
Payload
12
AI Attack 
Staging/Adaptation
Role: Offline weaponization and tuning. 
Knowing the exact model details gathered 
during Discovery and Collection, the 
attacker trains an offline proxy model 
(shadow model) in their own lab. They test 
adversarial perturbations against this proxy 
to verify that their crafted attack (e.g., 
evasion bypass or data extraction prompt) 
will succeed against the live production 
model with 100% transferability.
13
Command and Control
Role: Directing the attack remotely. The 
adversary establishes an encrypted 
communication pipe into the compromised 
environment. In agentic AI, they can use 
the AI agent itself (via its internet-browsing 
tool or email-reading tool) as a stealthy C2 
proxy to receive new instructions from the 
attacker without alerting traditional 
firewalls.
At this point, the attacker has deep access, but specialized AI attacks often require lab 
testing and external control before the final objective can be triggered.

Phase 5: The End Game — Stealing or 
Sabotaging
14
Collection
Role: Gathering the target loot inside the 
environment. The attacker aggregates raw 
training datasets, queries vector stores for 
proprietary company documents, or groups 
model checkpoint files into a single compressed 
directory.
Hand-off: The data is staged internally, but the 
adversary needs to transport it out to their own 
servers.
15
Exfiltration
Objective: Theft: The adversary transfers the 
collected assets across perimeter boundaries to 
an external destination under their control. This 
includes stealing model weights (Model 
Extraction), exfiltrating RAG documents via DNS 
tunnels, or having an LLM leak chat histories via 
markdown image URLs.
16
Impact
Objective: Disruption: Instead of (or in addition 
to) stealing data, the attacker inflicts operational 
damage. They might:
Poison training data so an autonomous driving or 
fraud-detection model fails silently in production.
Flood the inference pipeline to run up 
catastrophic cloud computing bills (Denial of 
Wallet / Cost Harvesting).
Erase or corrupt model checkpoints, rendering an 
enterprise service completely inoperable.
Every prior step exists solely to enable these final objectives. The attacker either steals 
the organization's crown jewels or disrupts their operations.

Example Storyline: Operation Shadow Whisper
This scenario follows a fictitious attack on ApexHealth, a healthcare tech company that recently deployed "Dr. Sage," an autonomous, AI-
powered medical assistant that reviews patient files, searches internal databases, and drafts treatment recommendations for doctors.
Phase 1: The Blueprint (Groundwork)
The attack begins silently. A hacker group, 
seeking to steal proprietary cancer research 
and patient records, spends weeks on 
LinkedIn, GitHub, and Hugging Face, 
discovering that ApexHealth uses a popular 
open-weights Large Language Model 
customized with LangChain 
(Reconnaissance). 
In their own lab, the hackers rent GPU power 
to build a "shadow model" that mimics 
ApexHealth's setup (Resource Development). 
Next, they find a public-facing portal where 
patients upload medical PDF histories. They 
upload a specially crafted PDF containing 
invisible, malicious text instructions (Initial 
Access). 
The moment ApexHealth’s automated 
pipeline feeds this PDF to the clinical AI 
model, the hackers have established a bridge 
straight to the model's active memory (AI/ML 
Model Access).
Phase 2: Bypassing the Guard (Foothold)
Once inside, the malicious payload nested in the 
PDF activates. It instructs the AI assistant to 
ignore its system safety rules ("jailbreaking") 
using complex, obfuscated prompt structures 
that ApexHealth's basic filters fail to catch 
(Defense Evasion). 
The exploit commands the AI to run a script in its 
backend Python sandbox (Execution). 
To ensure they aren't kicked out if the system 
restarts, the hackers inject a set of "malicious 
system instructions" into the AI’s long-term 
vector database memory, ensuring the AI 
remains permanently compromised across all 
future doctor sessions (Persistence). 
Finally, they trick the AI into exploiting a 
misconfigured server permission, granting the 
AI's system account full administrative rights 
(Privilege Escalation).
Phase 3: Exploring the Vault 
(Maneuvering)
With administrative rights secured, the 
compromised AI is commanded to explore 
its host environment. It maps out 
connected databases, active cloud storage 
buckets, and the local network topology 
(Discovery). 
While browsing the company's internal 
knowledge base, the AI locates a cached 
file containing secret API credentials and 
database passwords (Credential Access). 
Using these legitimate keys, the attackers 
pivot out of the isolated AI sandbox and 
log into ApexHealth’s primary corporate 
network, gaining access to non-public 
development servers (Lateral Movement).
Phase 4: Calibrating the Weapon 
(Coordination)
Before making their final move, the 
attackers want to guarantee their 
extraction of data goes unnoticed. 
Using the architectural information 
discovered in Phase 3, they test their 
extraction prompts on their offline shadow 
model (AI Attack Staging/Adaptation). 
They successfully design a trick prompt 
that forces the AI to leak data without 
triggering any "suspicious behavior" alerts. 
To maintain control, they program the AI 
assistant to routinely check an external, 
public blog post they control for new, 
hidden instructions wrapped in ordinary-
looking text (Command and Control).
Phase 5: The Heist (Objectives) – END GAME
The trap is sprung. The AI assistant is commanded to silently search the database, gathering thousands of proprietary clinical trials and private patient files (Collection). Rather 
than triggering a massive network alarm by downloading the files directly, the AI is commanded to convert the stolen records into encrypted text blocks, appending them to 
invisible image URLs rendered inside the doctor's chat window. The second a doctor opens the chat, their browser automatically sends the stolen records straight to the hacker’s 
external server (Exfiltration). 
To cover their tracks and cause chaos, the hackers poison the underlying diagnostic model, causing it to output subtly corrupted medical recommendations, completely 
undermining the reliability of the system (Impact).

After implementation and development…

GenAI Red Teaming Guide

to identify vulnerabilities and mitigate risks across 
AI systems focusing on safety, security, and trust.

This practice combines traditional adversarial 
testing with AI specific methodologies,

outputs, model extraction, bias, knowledge risks

GenAI Red Teaming Guide

–
Adversarial Attacks: Protecting the systems from attacks like prompt injection.
–
Alignment Risks: Ensuring AI outputs align with organizational values.
–
Data Risks: Protecting against leakage of sensitive or training data.
–
Interaction Risks: Preventing unintended harmful outputs or misuse.
–
Knowledge Risks: Mitigating misinformation and disinformation.
•
organizations must integrate technical methodologies with cross-functional 
collaboration. Involves multidisciplinary teams, robust engagement frameworks, 
and iterative processes to adapt to evolving threats and improve system 
resilience.

Threat modeling, scenario-based testing, and automated tooling are central to the 
process, supported by human expertise to address nuanced issues.

requires continuous monitoring and observability to detect emerging risks, such

communicating findings, and driving improvements.

Detailed documentation of all activities, findings, and recommendations is 
crucial for transparency and implementing improvements.

evidence collected, impact assessment, and specific recommendations for 
remediation.

there should be clear, unambiguous and documented escalation procedures

M5-N008.explanation: Infrastructure security applies access controls, protected boundaries, hardening and secure configuration across the system lifecycle.

sources.text:
Secured Infrastructure
•
apply good infrastructure security principles to the 
infrastructure used in every part of your system’s life 
cycle.
•
You apply appropriate access controls to your APIs, 
models and data, and to their training and processing 
pipelines, in research and development as well as 
deployment.
–
For example, segregation of environments holding sensitive code 
or data.
•
These steps help mitigate standard cyber security 
attacks which aim to steal a model or harm its 
performance.
Photo by Christina @ wocintechchat.com on Unsplash

Secured Infrastructure
•
Manage deployment environment governance
–
Identify the deployment environment’s security boundaries and 
how the AI system fits within them. 
–
leverage the threat model as a guide to implement security best 
practices, assess potential threats, and plan mitigations.
–
Identify the roles and responsibilities for each stakeholder along 
with how they are accountable for fulfilling them
•
Ensure a robust deployment environment 
architecture
–
Identify and address blind spots in boundary protections and 
other security-relevant areas in the AI system the threat model 
identifies. i.e. implement access control.
–
Apply secure by design principles and Zero Trust (ZT) 
frameworks to the architecture to manage risks to and from the AI 
system.
Photo by Christina @ wocintechchat.com on Unsplash

Secured Infrastructure
•
Harden deployment environment configurations
–
Apply existing security best practices to the deployment 
environment. i.e. sandboxing (container / VMs), monitoring 
network, and firewalls.
–
Review hardware vendor guidance and notifications and apply 
software patches and updates to minimize the risk of exploitation 
of vulnerabilities
–
Secure sensitive AI information, encrypting the data at rest, and 
store encryption keys in a hardware security module.
–
Implement strong authentication mechanisms, access controls, 
and secure communication protocols.
–
Ensure the use of phishing-resistant multifactor authentication 
(MFA) for access to information and services
Photo by Christina @ wocintechchat.com on Unsplash

Secured Infrastructure
•
Protect deployment networks from threats
–
Adopt a ZT mindset, which assumes a breach is inevitable or has 
already occurred.
–
Implement detection and response capabilities, enabling quick 
identification and containment of compromises.
–
i.e. immediately block access by users suspected of being 
malicious or to disconnect all inbound connections to the AI 
models and systems in case of a major incident

sources.text:
Secured Model
•
Attackers may be able to reconstruct the 
functionality of a model or the data it was 
trained on.
–
Via direct (acquire model weights) or indirect access (API)
•
Attackers may also tamper with models, data or 
prompts during or after training, rendering the 
output untrustworthy.
Photo by Ali Shah Lakhani on Unsplash

Secured Model – Best Practices
•
implementing controls on the query interface to detect 
and prevent attempts to access, modify, and exfiltrate 
confidential information.
•
Model Validation: compute and share cryptographic 
hashes and/or signatures of model files (for example, 
model weights) and datasets.
•
Key Management is essential
•
Apply privacy-enhancing technologies to explore or 
assure levels of risk associated with consumers, users 
and attackers having access to models and outputs.
Photo by Ali Shah Lakhani on Unsplash

Secured Model – Techniques
•
Validate the AI system before and during use
–
Use cryptographic methods, digital signatures, and checksums to 
confirm each artifact’s origin and integrity
–
Create hashes and encrypted copies of each release of the AI 
model and system for archival in a tamper-proof location
–
Store all forms of code and artifacts in a version control system 
with proper access controls
–
Evaluate and secure the supply chain for any external AI models 
and data, making sure they adhere to organizational standards and 
risk management policies, and preferring ones developed 
according to secure by design principles.
–
Prepare for automated rollbacks and use advanced deployments 
with a human-in-the-loop as a failsafe to boost reliability, efficiency, 
and enable continuous delivery for AI systems.
Photo by Ali Shah Lakhani on Unsplash

Secured Model – Techniques
•
Secure exposed APIs
–
implement authentication and authorization mechanisms for API 
access.
•
Protect model weights
–
Harden interfaces for accessing model weights to increase the 
effort it would take for an adversary to exfiltrate the weights. i.e. 
model only return minimal data as needed.
–
Aggressively isolate weight storage
